title: The question that draws out faith and the fountain greater than the pool
english: He was not ignorant of what they wanted. The matter was plain. But he drew the gift out of their own words, so that by their words they might be justified. Surely the one who knows hearts does not fail to understand what is said. Rather, he waited for the word, so that the asking might draw on the working. So also in this case, the physician stood beside the man and came over to the one who was worn out. And it is no wonder that he came to the one lying by the pool, since he had come over from heaven to us. He asked him: "Do you want to be made well?" (John 5:6). By the question he was drawing him toward knowledge and rousing him to ask. It was the gift of a great grace, for it was without pay. That is why the man had the healer come over to him of his own accord. And the man said to him: "Yes, Lord. The long duration of my illnesses makes health desirable to me, and I do desire it, but I have no one to help me."

Do not be discouraged, man, because you have no human helper. You have God standing beside you. In one respect he is human, in another respect God, for both must be confessed. Confessing the humanity is of no benefit if the divinity is not confessed along with it. Rather, it brings a curse. For cursed is the one who has hope in a human being (Jeremiah 17:5). If, then, we who hope in Jesus were hoping in a human being and not weaving the divinity together with our hope, we would be heirs of a curse. But as it is, we confess both God and human, and both truly. He is truly God, begotten from a true Father, and truly human, begotten not in appearance but in truth. Worshiping him, we await true salvation.

"I do want to be made well, but I have no one to help me." See whether, where salvation was lacking, he did not give the working there. For many of the sick had houses, and also acquaintances, and others besides. But this man, truly afflicted in every kind of poverty and having no power of help from outside, left utterly alone, had as his helper the only-begotten Son of God. "Do you want to be made well?" "Yes, Lord, but I have no one to help me, so that when the water is stirred, he may put me into the pool" (John 5:7). You have the fountain, because with you is the fountain of life (Psalm 36:9; LXX 35:10), a fountain that makes fountains. "Whoever drinks of this water, rivers will flow from his belly" (John 7:38). Not water flowing downward, but water leaping up. For what belongs to Jesus does not make it spring from above downward, but from earthly things toward heavenly things. Water leaping up into eternal life (John 4:14). For Jesus is the fountain of good things.

And why do you wait for a pool? You have the one who walks on the waters, the rebuker of winds, the charioteer of the sea. He not only had the sea spread beneath him like a pavement, but also granted to Peter the same power of walking. For when it was a lightless night and the light was present but not recognized, Jesus walking on the waters was unknown as far as the appearance of his form showed, but the distinctive quality of his voice revealed who was there. They thought he was a ghost and were afraid. Jesus said to them: "It is I; do not be afraid" (Matthew 14:27). Peter says to him: "If you are the one I know, or rather, the one the Father revealed to me, command me to come to you on the waters" (Matthew 14:28). And he said to him with most generous sharing: "Come" (Matthew 14:29).

So then, the charioteer and maker of the waters was present by the waters of the pool. To him the paralytic says: "I have no one to help me, so that when the water is stirred, he may put me into the pool." The Savior says to him: "Why do you wait for the stirring of waters? Be healed without stirring. Why do you wait for a visible movement? By a word the command comes to pass, swifter than thought. Only look at the working of the fountain and suspect that the one appearing in flesh is God. Do not consider the one who appears, but the one working through what appears." "I have no one to help me, so that when the water is stirred, he may put me into the pool." And he says to him: "Why do you wait for small things? Why do you seek healing from waters?" "Rise," the Resurrection said to you. For everywhere the Savior becomes all things to all people: bread to the hungry, water to the thirsty, resurrection to the dead, physician to the sick, redemption to sinners.

"Rise, take up your mat, and walk" (John 5:8). But first rise. First cast off the disease. Then take up the sinew of faith. First gain strength against the mat that carried you, and learn to carry with a wooden vessel what you long revered. And that Savior commanded him to carry the wooden litter. He is the one of whom it is said: "The king made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon. He made its posts of silver, its back of purple, and within it a stone pavement" (Song of Songs 3:9-10).

orientation: Cyril is explaining why Jesus asked the blind men and now the paralytic what they wanted, and he is about to contrast the pool's water with Christ as the fountain of life.

title: The Song's symbols of the passion and the healing's unbelief
english: The symbols of the passion are stored up in the Song of Songs—nuptial, sober, and chaste. Do not take the words according to the common assumption and, fixing your gaze on nothing, suppose the songs are erotic and passionate. No: the words are nuptial, filled with chastity. And if you do not understand the Song of Songs, come to the Proverbs, and by a path and by steps ascend to those heights. "Wisdom built herself a house"—the text speaks as if about a woman—"and sent out her servants" (Proverbs 9:1-3). And again elsewhere it says: "Love her, and she will keep you" (Proverbs 4:6). This is not love of a woman, but of wisdom, which drives out erotic love. For where wisdom is possessed, there erotic love is banished. For the passions are not in keeping with wisdom; rather, the thoughts are wise. "They became lust-mad horses"—the impulse is without reason. So when you hear in the Song of Songs words spoken as if about a bridegroom and a bride, do not fall to the ground, and do not listen to them with passion. Use what is free of passion to retrain the passions.

Meditate, then, on the divine songs, filled with chastity and revealing the passion of Christ. For the passages that narrate the Savior's passion also name the place: "He entered into a garden," because of the one buried there. And it mentioned the spices: "He took my myrrh in full measure"—for the dispensation was fulfilled. And after the resurrection it said: "I ate my bread with my honey" (Song of Songs 5:1). For they gave him a piece of honeycomb. And the Song of Songs spoke again about the wine mixed with myrrh: "I will give you to drink of the spiced wine" (Song of Songs 8:2). And about the ointment poured on his head it said elsewhere: "While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance" (Song of Songs 1:12). For while he reclined in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came in and broke an alabaster jar of pure and costly nard and poured it over his head.

So also concerning the cross. The litter is the wood of the cross, the thing that carries. "He made its posts of silver." The beginning of the cross was silver—the betrayal. For just as a very beautiful house has a golden roof laid on top, while the posts hold up the whole structure, so also the beginning of Christ's crucifixion and resurrection was silver. For if Judas had not betrayed him, he would not have been crucified. Therefore, because the beginning of the renowned passion was silver, "he made its posts of silver."

"Its back of purple." For this reason they also clothed him in purple—mocking, yes, but acting prophetically. For he was a king. Even if they acted in mockery, still they acted; and it became the symbol of royal dignity. And if the crown was of thorns, still it was a crown, and one plaited by soldiers. For kings are proclaimed by soldiers. "Its back of purple, and within it a stone pavement." The diligent members of the church know the stone pavement, the one called Gabbatha, which is in Pilate's court.

I have said these things in a digression from the mat, having come to the litter. So he said to him: "Rise, take up your mat and walk" (John 5:8). The disease was long-lasting, but the remedy was swift. The paralysis was many years old, but the strengthening of sinews was swift. For the maker of sinews, the one who provides varied remedies for the blind, the one who through an anointing of mud paradoxically granted the plaster—if mud is poured on someone who sees, it hinders seeing; but Jesus through mud granted sight to those who could not see. And for others again the power came through other means. To this one he said: "Rise, take up your mat and walk."

How great do you suppose the astonishment was that seized the onlookers? But the sight was marvelous, and the unbelief was terrible. A disease of many years was healed, but unbelief of long standing was not healed. The Jews persisted in their afflictions, and they did not wish to be healed.

They ought to have been astonished at what happened; they ought to have worshiped the physician of souls and bodies. But they grumbled. For they were descendants of grumblers, those who twist good things into evil, who call the bitter sweet and the sweet bitter. But Jesus worked with full divine purpose on the Sabbath, doing what is above the Sabbath, so that the work might persuade. For since word fights against word, but a work is beyond dispute, he healed on the Sabbath, teaching—so that the word might not become a matter of dispute, but the work might persuade those who saw.

They kept saying: "It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your mat" (John 5:10). The lawgiver was present, and someone else was saying "It is not lawful for you." "Appoint, Lord, a lawgiver over them" (Psalm 9:20 LXX)—this was said about the Savior.

orientation: Cyril is explaining that the Song of Songs' nuptial imagery is a sober prophecy of Christ's passion, then returns to the healing of the paralytic and the Jews' unbelief.

title: The healed man's defense and the call to sin no more
english: The man who had just now been healed in both soul and body received a wise word from Wisdom, and he answers at once. He does not answer in a legalistic way, but makes his reply brief. "You all know," he says, "my long-lasting illness and my many years of lying down, the helplessness of my misery. Not one of you ever showed a caring act by taking me and putting me first into the pool so that I might be healed. And yet, when you showed no caring act then, how have you now taken up the lawgiving role, saying, 'It is not lawful for you to carry your mat'? I make my answer to you very brief: the one who made me well is the one who told me. If you despise me, let the deed itself amaze you. He applied no plaster; he used no medical devices or remedies. He spoke a word, and the work followed. He commanded, and I am carrying out the command. I have become obedient to the command of the one who healed me by commands. For if the one who commanded had been powerless in his commands to bring about the healing, there would have been no need to obey them. But since by words he commanded a long-lasting affliction to cease, and it clearly did, I am most justly obedient to the one whose command even the illness heard and departed. The one who made me well is the one who told me, 'Take up your mat.'"

The healed man did not know who the healer was. Here the humility of our Savior is on full display. For after healing him, Jesus slipped away so that he would not be recognized for the healing. But we do exactly the opposite. If we ever happen to see visions, or help with our hands, or drive out a demon by invocation, we are so far from hiding the success that we boast even when no one asks. But Jesus, teaching us by his deeds not to speak about ourselves, granted the healing and at the same time slipped away so that he would not be recognized, withdrawing at the right time and being present at the right time. For when the praise of the success needed to be kept quiet, then he withdraws. But when the crowds had dispersed, so that along with the bodily healing he might also bring healing to the soul, then he was present and said: "See, you have become well; sin no more."

He is a varied physician: sometimes he heals the soul first and then the body, and sometimes the reverse. "Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you." Through one man he teaches many. For the word was not spoken to that man alone, but to all of us as well. For if we ever fall into afflictions or sorrows or hardships, let no one blame God. For God cannot be tempted by evils, and he himself tempts no one. Each of us is scourged when he is bound fast by the cords of his own sins. "Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you." Let every person hear this saying: the one who was committing fornication before, let him put away the passion; the one who was greedy before, become merciful. Let the robber hear: sin no more. Great is God's willingness to forgive wrongs, and abundant is his grace. But do not take the excess of his forbearance as a provision for contempt, and do not sin just because God is patient. Rather, be healed now of the fleshly passions, and say for yourself the words read at the right moment: "For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions aroused through the law were at work in our members" (Romans 7:5). But when the apostle says "when we were in the flesh," he does not mean this flesh that we are clothed in, but fleshly deeds. He was still wearing flesh when he said, "when we were in the flesh." But just as when the flood was about to be brought on, God said, "My spirit shall not remain in these people, because they are flesh," the spirit being changed into a fleshly choice, so also here the apostle says, "when we were in the flesh."

Let no one, then, be in the flesh; but while being in the flesh, let him not walk according to the flesh. For the apostle does not want us to avoid doing evil by taking ourselves completely out of the world; rather, while we are in the flesh, he wants us to enslave the flesh and not be ruled by it. Let us not be enslaved; let us rule. Let us use food in due measure, not being carried away by gluttony, but bridling the stomach so that we may also rule over the desires below it. Let the body be ruled by the soul, and let the soul not be dragged away by fleshly pleasures. "Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you." The word proclaims this to all, and may all ears hear it. For not every hearing of the flesh that receives the word already receives it into the mind. That is why the Savior said: "Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear," speaking to those who have ears of flesh.
Let everyone, then, hear Jesus and sin no more, but let us run to the one who forgives sins.

orientation: The healed man, given a wise reply by Wisdom, answers the Jews who object to his carrying the mat on the Sabbath, and Cyril then applies Jesus' command 'sin no more' to all hearers.
